message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear).
• Landlords must provide a written itemized list of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease, move‑in inspection report, and any receipts for repairs.
• Request a written receipt for the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a habitable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural safety).
• If the landlord fails to maintain habitability, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or terminate the lease. | • Document problems with photos and written notices.
• Give the landlord a reasonable time to fix issues before taking further action. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlords can raise rent at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• No statutory cap on rent increases. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses.
• Ask for a written notice of any increase. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must provide a valid reason (e.g., non‑payment, violation of lease) and follow the notice requirements. | • Keep copies of all notices.
• If you’re evicted, you have the right to contest the eviction in court. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• After the notice period, the landlord can file an unlawful detainer action.
• You have the right to a hearing and to present evidence. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you receive an eviction notice, consider contacting a tenant‑rights group or attorney. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlords must give reasonable notice (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Discrimination** | • Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Property Code, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income. | • Report discriminatory practices to the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, provided you follow the proper procedure (written notice, reasonable time, receipts). | • Keep receipts and document the defect. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease. Late fees are allowed only if stated in the lease. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if needed. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • The lease may restrict subletting; if allowed, you must follow the lease terms. | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify which utilities you are responsible for. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Maintenance Responsibilities** | • Tenants must keep the unit clean and free of damage. | • Perform routine maintenance (e.g., changing light bulbs, cleaning filters). | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) provides tenant‑rights guides.
• Local tenant‑rights organizations (e.g., Texas Tenants Union).
• Legal aid clinics for low‑income tenants. | • Contact these resources if you need help with disputes or legal representation. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – look for clauses on rent, security deposit, maintenance, entry, and termination. 2. **Ask for a written itemized list of any deductions** you might owe at move‑out. 3. **Confirm the landlord’s obligations** for repairs and habitability. 4. **Verify the lease’s notice periods** for rent increases or termination. 5. **Check for any discrimination clauses** or restrictions that might violate fair housing laws. --- #### When Things Go Wrong - **Document everything**: photos, videos, written notices, emails, and receipts. - **Serve written notices** to the landlord for any complaints. - **Keep copies** of all correspondence. - **Seek help early**: contact a tenant‑rights organization or legal aid if you face eviction or other disputes. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is for general educational purposes and does not constitute legal advice. Laws can change, and specific circumstances may alter your rights. If you have a particular issue, consider consulting a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights group.
